chapter_theme: The ascetics bring the Chola king news of his son's death indirectly, through old stories of Kakandi in which men who desired chaste women were punished by the spirit's warning or by Kakandhan's own sword, and through a tale of lifelong chastity and charity; asked for the present case, they tell how the prince's ripened deed killed him, and the king calls the killing his own duty done by another, orders the body burned in secret and Manimekalai put under guard.

cast.role: those who worship at the old woman's shrine (முதியோள் கோட்டம்) beside the burning ground
the ascetics of the Chakravala shrine, who carry the news of the prince's death to the king
one of those ascetics, who tells the king the old stories of Kakandi
Madhavi's daughter, a young renunciant, in whose disguised presence the prince was killed
the Chola prince, killed in the hall by the vidyadhara's sword
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
the king's general, to whom he gives his orders
the Chola king of old who hid from Parasurama and left the city in Kakandhan's keeping
Kanthan's son by a courtesan, keeper of the city named Kakandi after him, who kills both his sons
Kakandhan's son who called the brahmin wife Maruthi to him and was killed by his father
Kakandhan's elder son, who seized the aged Visakai's garland and was killed by his father
a brahmin wife of Kakandi whom Kakandhan's son desired
the great spirit of the Bhuta crossroads (பூத சதுக்கம்) of Puhar
a merchant's son of Kakandi, cousin of Visakai, who vows to love no other woman
Dharmadattan's cousin (his maternal uncle's daughter), slandered with him, who stays unmarried for life
Dharmadattan's father and mother, who leave the city with him
the speaking image painted on the pillar of the Ulaka Aravi hall
a brahmin of southern Madurai who sends Dharmadattan home
Chithirapathi's daughter, Manimekalai's mother, a Buddhist renunciant
Kayachandikai's vidyadhara husband, who killed the prince

manimekalai:22:1-18.reading: At dawn the worshippers at the old woman's shrine tell the ascetics of the Chakravala shrine what happened to Udayakumaran; the ascetics ask Manimekalai, who tells them unshaken, and then, hiding her with the prince's body, they go to the palace, have themselves announced, and bless the king's umbrella, spear, sceptre, wheel and years.
manimekalai:22:1-18.nuance: The ascetics come to the king with a death in which he is implicated, yet open only with blessing; the news itself is withheld for two hundred lines. Lines 11-12 (கோயில் மன்னனைக் குறுகினர் சென்று) use the formula with which Kannaki is brought before the Pandya in Silappathikaram 20.
manimekalai:22:1-18.unit_note: End moved from line 16 to line 18: the blessing that begins at line 13 closes with வாழிய வேந்தே at line 18.
manimekalai:22:1-18.event: The ascetics of the Chakravala shrine learn of the prince's death, hear Manimekalai's account, hide her with the body, and go to the palace to bless the king.

manimekalai:22:19-38.reading: One ascetic tells the king that not only today but of old men who, drunk with lust, approached chaste wives or sent their hearts after women of penance have died when their evil deed ripened, and begins with old Kakandi: King Kanthan, told by the virgin goddess to keep out of Parasurama's sight, called Kakandhan, his son by the city's courtesan, to guard the town, since one with no right to rule would not draw Parasurama, and the town was named Kakandi.
manimekalai:22:19-38.nuance: The general claim is made before any example, and widened from the chaste wife to the woman of penance (நல் தவப் பெண்டிர், 22), which is where Udayakumaran stands. The Kanthan story explains the town's name and introduces Kakandhan, whose lack of a right to rule (33) is what protects him; who the virgin goddess (கன்னி, 27) is, the unit does not say.
manimekalai:22:19-38.unit_note: Start moved from line 17 to 19 (the blessing ends at 18) and end from 37 to 38, where the naming of the town (இயைந்த நாமம் இப் பதிக்கு இட்டு) completes Kanthan's speech; line 39 still links Kanthan's departure to the next story.
manimekalai:22:19-38.event: King Kanthan, to hide from Parasurama, leaves the city in the keeping of Kakandhan, his courtesan's son, and names it Kakandi.

claims.claim: men who in lust approach chaste wives or set their hearts on women ascetics die when their evil deed ripens

manimekalai:22:39-56.reading: Kakandhan's son, seeing the brahmin wife Maruthi returning alone from her Kaveri bath, calls her to him; she reasons that rain-bringing wives never enter another man's heart, so having entered his she is no longer fit to tend her husband's three fires, will not go home, and at the Bhuta's crossroads protests that she did no wrong against her husband, kept the household chastity that brings rain, and does not know her fault, and asks whether the god there is false.
manimekalai:22:39-56.nuance: Maruthi condemns herself for something that happened only in the youth's mind (கண்டோன் நெஞ்சில் கரப்பு எளிதாயினேன், 52): the fault she cannot name is not an act but having been desirable, and the rule that excludes her from the fire rite is one she applies to herself before anyone accuses her.
manimekalai:22:39-56.unit_note: Start moved from 38 to 39 and end from 57 to 56: Maruthi's lament closes with அரற்றலும் at 56; line 57 begins the Bhuta's appearance and speech.
manimekalai:22:39-56.event: Kakandhan's son calls the brahmin wife Maruthi to him at the river; distraught, she goes not home but to the Bhuta's crossroads and accuses its god.

claims.claim: wives whose word brings rain never enter another man's heart
a wife who has entered another man's heart may no longer tend her husband's three sacred fires

manimekalai:22:57-79.reading: The great Bhuta appears and tells Maruthi that she has not trusted the poet who never lies on the wife who worships her husband rather than a god, that her love of riddles, gossip and drum-loud festivals and her duty to worship gods have cost her the power to command rain and to scorch the hearts of others as steadfast women do, that if she gives these up the rain will obey her, that its noose will not bind her as it binds straying wives, and that its own justice comes only after the king's seven days, within which Kakandhan will cut down the youth; on the day it named, the youth is killed by his father's sword.
manimekalai:22:57-79.nuance: The Bhuta does not blame her for the youth's desire; it blames her worship of gods, festivals and talk, taking the couplet's தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் literally. It also sets an order of justice: the king's punishment first, the spirit's only if the king fails within seven days (72-73), and the king does not fail.
manimekalai:22:57-79.unit_note: Start moved from 58 to 57 so the Bhuta's appearance and speech stay together; end moved from 68 (mid-speech) to 79, where the narrator reports the youth's death; 80-81 open the next story.
manimekalai:22:57-79.event: The Bhuta appears to Maruthi, explains her lost power and foretells the youth's punishment; within the seven days his father kills him with the sword.

claims.claim: a wife who rises worshipping her husband rather than a god can bid the rain fall
a wife given to festivals, gossip and the worship of gods loses the power to command rain
the spirit's punishment follows only when the king's justice has failed within seven days

echoes.words: தெய்வம் தொழா அள் கொழுநன் தொழுது எழுவாள்

manimekalai:22:80-98.reading: The ascetic goes on: the cousins Dharmadattan and Visakai were so beautiful that the whole town said they were fit for a lovers' marriage; Visakai left her house, climbed into the Ulaka Aravi hall, asked the image painted on its pillar to clear the slander, and when the speaking image told the city that she is a woman who brings rain, vowed that, since only a god's word could clear the town's mind, she would be her cousin's wife in her next birth and not join him in this one.
manimekalai:22:80-98.nuance: The image clears her by naming her a rain-bringer (மழை தரும் இவள், 93), the very power Maruthi lost; yet Visakai answers vindication with renunciation, as if the god's word cleared her name but not the occasion for talk.
manimekalai:22:80-98.unit_note: Start moved from 82 to 80: lines 80-81 (இன்னும் கேளாய் ... மன்னவர் ஏறே) address the king to open this second story.
manimekalai:22:80-98.event: Slandered with her cousin, Visakai goes to the pillar image in the Ulaka Aravi, which proclaims her chaste, and vows not to marry him in this birth.

manimekalai:22:99-114.reading: Visakai tells her mother and shuts herself in the maidens' chamber; Dharmadattan and his parents leave the city praising the image and settle in southern Madurai, where he vows to cherish no woman but Visakai and to let this birth go, and grows so rich in trade that the king gives him the etti flower, until he has reached sixty.
manimekalai:22:99-114.nuance: His vow mirrors hers from the other side: she refuses him in this birth, he refuses every other woman, so both give up this birth's marriage and keep the bond.
manimekalai:22:99-114.unit_note: End moved from 116 to 114: the brahmin's speech beginning at 115 runs to 120.
manimekalai:22:99-114.event: Visakai enters the maidens' chamber; Dharmadattan leaves with his parents for southern Madurai, vows to love no other woman, and grows rich and honoured until old age.

manimekalai:22:115-126.reading: A brahmin asks the rich Dharmadattan what he has done with his life, whether he has heard that those without a chaste wife do not enter the world of the gods however many good deeds they do, and bids him go home at once; he leaves Madurai and returns, and Visakai, hearing of it, comes out of her house and, unashamed before the crowd, goes to him.
manimekalai:22:115-126.nuance: The brahmin's saying makes a wife a man's condition for heaven; the next unit has Visakai answer it, putting virtue alone in that place (137-138). The school tag follows the speaker, a brahmin quoting a maxim; the unit names no text.
manimekalai:22:115-126.unit_note: Start moved from 117 to 115 (the brahmin's speech begins there) and end from 131 to 126, before Visakai's speech starts at 127.
manimekalai:22:115-126.event: A brahmin sends the aged Dharmadattan home to marry, and Visakai goes out before the crowd to meet him.

claims.claim: men without a chaste wife do not reach the world of the gods however many good deeds they do

manimekalai:22:127-142.reading: Visakai tells Dharmadattan that they never knew each other, asks where the beauty that bewildered them has hidden now that he is sixty and his hair is grey, says she will not come to his feet in this birth but will serve him in the next, reminds him that youth, body and wealth do not last and that sons do not give heaven, only great virtue being a true companion, and bids him give; he shows her his wealth, and the good they did together outnumbers the stars.
manimekalai:22:127-142.nuance: She addresses him as a householder without a wife (உளன் இல்லாள, 132), granting the brahmin's premise only to answer it: not a wife and not sons but virtue is the companion, and the two do their charity together while keeping her vow apart. The narrator's count (more than the stars) endorses her.
manimekalai:22:127-142.unit_note: Start moved from 132 to 127, where Visakai's speech begins, and end from 151 to 142, where the narration of their shared charity closes; 143 begins the elder son's story.
manimekalai:22:127-142.event: Visakai refuses marriage in this birth but turns the aged Dharmadattan to charity, which they practise together.

claims.claim: youth, the body and wealth do not last
sons do not win heaven for a man; only great virtue is a lasting companion

manimekalai:22:143-158.reading: As the aged virgin, cleared of slander by the god's grace, walks the bannered street, Kakandhan's elder son, whose brother died over Maruthi, burns with desire, takes the garland from her hair saying this is the marriage the ancients spoke of, and lifts it to wear; his raised hand will not come away from his hair, and Kakandhan, hearing it was for this woman, in fierce anger and without regard for his grief as a father, strikes his son with his sword.
manimekalai:22:143-158.nuance: The second son repeats the first son's offence against a woman now old, and claims an ancient form of marriage for it; the miracle answers him before the father does. Kakandhan, himself only a keeper of the city with no right to rule, twice executes his own son, which is the example the ascetic is preparing for the king. Whose head the hand sticks to turns on குஞ்சி (154), usually a man's hair, and on what இடுவான் (152) takes as object; the reading here takes it as his own.
manimekalai:22:143-158.unit_note: Start moved from 152 to 143 and end from 175 to 158: the elder son's story runs from 143 to his death at 158; 159 returns to the frame.
manimekalai:22:143-158.event: Kakandhan's elder son seizes the aged Visakai's garland as a token of marriage, his hand sticks fast, and his father kills him with the sword.

claims.claim: taking a woman's garland and wearing it is the marriage the ancients described

manimekalai:22:159-176.reading: The ascetic closes with a blessing; the king, catching his 'not only today', asks whether such a deed has happened today too, and the ascetic answers that those who know the final truth name five things to be shunned, toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust, of which lust is hardest to throw off; ascetics renounce it as the shunning of all evil, and those who do not renounce it suffer in unbearable hell.
manimekalai:22:159-176.nuance: The king himself asks for the present case, so the verdict that follows comes from his mouth. The five match the Buddhist precepts, but the unit attributes them only to those who know the final truth (முடி பொருள் உணர்ந்தோர், 169), so the claims are tagged general.
manimekalai:22:159-176.unit_note: Start moved from 176 back to 159 and end set at 176: the sentence that begins நீங்கார் அன்றே (175) ends with உழப்போர் at 176.
manimekalai:22:159-176.event: The king asks whether such a deed has happened today, and an ascetic begins his answer with the five things to be shunned.

claims.claim: toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust are the five things to be shunned
lust is hardest to throw off, and who shuns it has shunned all evil
those who do not renounce lust suffer in unbearable hell

manimekalai:22:177-204.reading: The ascetic tells the king that Madhavi, unable to bear her lover's suffering, entered the monks' dwelling, that her young daughter Manimekalai, resolved on penance, begged from house to house and came to the hall, that the prince nevertheless followed her like a shadow and, fearless of the dark, came to the hall for her, where she had taken Kayachandikai's form; and that since his evil deed had ripened it brought her to the hall, led him there at midnight, called Kayachandikai's husband, deceived his mind with 'he came for the vidyadhara's wife', and cut the prince down by that man's sword.
manimekalai:22:177-204.nuance: The grammatical subject of the killing (எறிந்தது, 203) is the ripened evil deed of 193, not the vidyadhara, whose hand is only its instrument; the ascetic thus tells the father his son's death without naming a human culprit. Whether one ascetic or several speak (161, 168, 204) the text leaves open.
manimekalai:22:177-204.unit_note: The original units 176-192 and 193-215 broke mid-sentence; this unit runs from 177 to the closing மாதவன் உரைத்தலும் at 204, and the king's reply (205-215) is its own unit.
manimekalai:22:177-204.event: The ascetic tells the king how his son, pursuing Manimekalai to the hall by night, was killed by Kayachandikai's vidyadhara husband.

claims.claim: the prince's own ripened evil deed brought about his death, using the vidyadhara's hand

manimekalai:22:205-215.reading: The king turns to his general Chozhika Enathi and says that the vidyadhara did to the prince what the king himself should have done, that without a guardian's guarding there can be neither ascetics' vows nor women's chastity, and orders that before other kings hear that an evil-doer was born in the line of the king who did justice on his own son, the prince be put on the pyre and the courtesan's daughter be put under guard.
manimekalai:22:205-215.nuance: The king takes the ascetics' examples as meant, but his justice is half concealment: the body is to be burned before the story reaches other kings, and the girl, whom the stories have shown blameless, is imprisoned. தகவு இலன் (207) may say the vidyadhara is not at fault or that he lacked the standing to act; either way he goes unpunished. The ancestor 'who did justice on his son' (210) is the Chola of the calf whom Kannaki cites in Silappathikaram 20.
manimekalai:22:205-215.unit_note: Split from the original 193-215 at line 205, where the king's speech begins.
manimekalai:22:205-215.event: The king declares the vidyadhara's killing of his son a just act, orders the body burned and Manimekalai put under guard.

claims.claim: a king must punish his own son's wrong as he would any other's
without the guardian's protection there are no ascetics' vows and no women's chastity

links.note: Both scenes bring a death before a king with the same approach formula (கோயில் மன்னனைக் குறுகினர்/குறுகினள் சென்று): Kannaki to the Pandya, the ascetics to the Chola.
links.teaches: Kannaki uses the audience to accuse the king of her husband's death, while the ascetics, bringing a father news of his son's death, hide the body and wrap the news in blessing and old stories, so the same entrance shows two ways of telling a king a truth he is implicated in.

links.note: The couplet says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave the man who crosses into another's home; the ascetic says such men die when their evil deed ripens, and adds those who set their hearts on women ascetics.
links.teaches: The couplet's offence is entering a married woman's home; the epic extends it to desire for a renunciant woman, who has no husband's home to violate, and makes death, not lasting disgrace, the outcome.

gains.a: The ascetic's general charge gains the Kural's account of what such a man carries while he lives.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case beyond the married woman, the woman of penance, which its home-centred wording leaves out.

links.note: Sudhamathi, carried off by a vidyadhara, became unfit for the brahmins yet her father kept her; Maruthi, only desired by a youth, declares herself unfit for her husband's fires.
links.teaches: The epic twice lets the brahmin purity rule fall on a woman who did nothing; in Sudhamathi's case the father stays by her, while Maruthi excludes herself before anyone else does, so the rule is shown working inside the woman's own conscience.

links.note: The Bhuta quotes the couplet to Maruthi and explains her lost power by her worship of gods, festivals and talk.
links.teaches: The couplet states the wife's power as a fact; the epic uses it as a test a chaste woman fails, reads தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் literally as a ban on worshipping gods, and adds festivals and gossip, so the couplet becomes a rule with conditions that can be broken.

gains.a: Maruthi's loss of power gains a named authority, the poet who never lies, behind the Bhuta's verdict.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case that spells out what not worshipping a god excludes and what happens to the power when it is not kept.

links.note: Devanthi urges Kannaki to bathe in the sacred tanks and worship to win her husband back, and Kannaki refuses; the Bhuta tells Maruthi that worship of gods is what cost her the rain.
links.teaches: The Manimekalai's Bhuta supplies the doctrine behind Kannaki's refusal of the tanks in the Silappathikaram: a pathini's power rests on not turning to gods, so Kannaki's refusal is part of what makes her word able to burn Madurai.

links.note: In the Silappathikaram the Bhuta of the crossroads nooses and devours unchaste women who hide their wrong and men who desire others' wives; here the same Bhuta tells Maruthi its noose will not bind her and that it acts only after the king's seven days.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show the spirit's justice as a reserve behind the king's: it binds the hidden offender, spares the woman who was only desired, and waits seven days for the king to punish the man before acting itself.

links.note: The image on the pillar (கந்தின் ... பாவை) of the Ulaka Aravi proclaims Visakai chaste here; in kaathai 20 the same image tells Kanchanan that the woman before him is Manimekalai in disguise.
links.teaches: The pillar image is the city's witness for women: it once cleared a slandered virgin by declaring her a rain-bringer, and later declares the truth about a disguised renunciant, but in the second case its word comes after the sword has fallen.

links.note: The Silappathikaram's image in the court weeps without speaking (நாவொடு நவிலாது) when the king's sceptre bends; the Manimekalai's speaking image (நா உடைப் பாவை) proclaims a woman's innocence to the city.
links.teaches: Puhar's images serve as witnesses of justice in both epics, but one only weeps silently at a bent sceptre while the other speaks and clears a woman, so the pairing shows the speaking image as an active judge where the weeping one is only a sign.

links.note: Visakai vows in youth to be her cousin's wife only in the next birth; at sixty she tells him again she will not come to his feet in this birth but will serve him in the next.
links.teaches: The vow made to silence a slander outlives the slander by forty years, so what began as a defence of her name becomes the form their love takes, kept apart in body and joined in shared charity.

links.note: The couplet says women who obtain their husbands win great distinction in the world of the gods; the brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter it.
links.teaches: Taken together, the couplet and the brahmin's maxim make the wife and husband each the other's way to heaven, but the epic gives the maxim to a man urging a sixty-year-old to marry and then has Visakai deny it, so the reciprocal rule is shown as a pressure rather than a truth.

gains.a: The brahmin's maxim gains its counterpart in the couplet, which ties a woman's heaven to her husband.
gains.b: The couplet gains the reverse claim about men, and a scene in which that claim is answered.

links.note: The brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter the world of the gods however much good they do; Visakai says sons do not give that world and only great virtue is a companion.
links.teaches: The same phrase, புத்தேள் உலகம், is used for opposite conditions within twenty lines: the brahmin makes a wife necessary, Visakai makes virtue sufficient, and the narrator sides with her by counting their charity above the stars.

links.note: The couplet calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Visakai calls great virtue the true companion (விழுத் துணை) in place of youth, body, wealth and sons.
links.teaches: Visakai uses the couplet's idea of virtue as companion to replace the wife-companion the brahmin demanded, so a teaching about virtue outlasting death becomes an answer to the claim that a man needs marriage for heaven.

gains.a: Her answer gains the couplet's reason why virtue alone survives.
gains.b: The couplet's companion gains a concrete rival it displaces: the wife and the sons a householder is told he must have.

links.note: The quatrain says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounce in childhood; Visakai points to Dharmadattan's grey hair and turns him not to renunciation but to giving.
links.teaches: The quatrain offers only two paths, early renunciation or clinging to youth; Visakai, who has kept a vow of chastity since youth, shows a third for the grey-haired householder: shared charity without marriage.

gains.a: Visakai's appeal to his grey hair gains the quatrain's standard of what the wise do before it comes.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the one who saw age coming chose a vow and charity rather than the robe.

links.note: The couplet says evils will not touch a man for seven births if he has children of good character; Visakai says sons do not give heaven.
links.teaches: On the reading that the seven births are the parent's own, the couplet credits good children with protecting the parent beyond this life, which Visakai flatly denies, so the pair marks a point where the epic's teacher rejects a household hope the Kural endorses.

gains.a: Visakai's denial gains its target: a recognised claim that children carry merit to their parents.
gains.b: The couplet gains a direct contrary in a text that counts only one's own virtue.

links.note: Kakandhan, though grieving, kills his elder son with his own sword for seizing Visakai's garland; the present Chola says the vidyadhara did to his son what he himself should have done.
links.teaches: The ascetic's stories prepare the king's verdict: Kakandhan executes his sons with his own hand, and the Chola, faced with a son already dead, claims that act as his own duty, while also hiding the body from other kings, which Kakandhan never did.

links.note: Tirumular calls killing, theft, lust and lying sins as great as mountains, whose giving up leads to Siva's feet; the ascetic names toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust as the five to be shunned and threatens hell to those who keep lust.
links.teaches: Two traditions share nearly the same list of sins but use it differently: Tirumular makes their giving up a path to Siva's feet, while the ascetic names no god, singles out lust as the one that contains the rest, and uses the list to warn a king of hell.

gains.a: The ascetic's list gains a parallel that shows how far it is shared across schools.
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a godless version of the same discipline, where shunning is an end in itself and its failure leads to hell rather than away from Siva.

links.note: The prince follows Manimekalai like a shadow (நிழல் போல், 185); the couplet says ruin stays at the evildoer's feet like his shadow.
links.teaches: The epic inverts the couplet's shadow: the prince makes himself Manimekalai's shadow, but his own evil deed is the shadow at his own feet, and it catches him in the hall where he followed her.

gains.a: The prince's pursuit gains the couplet's image of what was following him.
gains.b: The couplet's shadow gains a scene where the pursuer is himself pursued, so the image shows how the ruin comes.

links.note: In kaathai 20 the pillar image tells Kanchanan that ripened karma took the prince's life; here the ascetic tells the king that the prince's evil deed itself struck him by the vidyadhara's hand.
links.teaches: The killing is told twice as the work of karma, but the deity also tells Kanchanan his act was a cruel deed that will follow him, while the ascetic, speaking to the father, leaves the killer's guilt out, so the same explanation is shaped by who hears it.

links.note: The pillar image tells Kanchanan he has done a cruel deed whose fruit will not leave him; the king says the vidyadhara did what the king should have done.
links.teaches: The same killing is a cruel deed with consequences in the deity's eyes and a royal duty done by another's hand in the king's, so the epic sets karmic judgment and royal justice side by side without reconciling them.

links.note: Kannaki cites the Chola who put his own son under the chariot wheel to shame the Pandya; the Chola king here fears it will be said that in that king's line an evil-doer was born.
links.teaches: The memory Kannaki used to accuse another king becomes a weight on the Chola's own line: he accepts his son's death as justice, but his first thought is to keep the stain on Manu's line from other kings, so the ancestor's example breeds concealment as well as justice.

links.note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the brahmins forget their books; the king says that without the guardian's guarding there are no ascetics' vows and no women's chastity.
links.teaches: The king adapts the couplet's list of what fails without a guardian to ascetics' vows and women's chastity, the two things his son violated, so the general rule becomes the reason he must count his own son's death as just.

gains.a: The king's maxim gains the couplet's frame of the guardian's duty, which shows it as a known rule rather than a private excuse.
gains.b: The couplet's list gains vows and chastity, and a case where the guardian's duty runs against his own son.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over nature, as the rain
